title: The Room
blurb: You have the job. Now you have one grey Saturday, and a week's pay you can't afford to lose, to find somewhere to live in a city that still doesn't know you.

text.A2: Mrs Halloran is brisk and grey-eyed. She shows you in. The room has good light off the water. But someone's things are still here, half-packed. A coat hangs on a hook. A tin of buttons sits on the sill. A box waits by the wall. Someone lived here, and lately, and left in a hurry.
text.B1: Mrs Halloran is brisk and grey-eyed, and shows you in without ceremony. The room has good light off the water. But someone's things are still here, half-packed: a coat on a hook, a tin of buttons on the sill, a box by the wall. Someone lived here lately, and left in a hurry.
text.B2: Mrs Halloran is brisk and grey-eyed, and shows you in without ceremony or small talk. The room has good, clean light off the water. But someone's things are still here, only half-packed: a coat left hanging on a hook, a tin of buttons on the sill, a box waiting by the wall. Someone lived here, and lately, and by the look of it left in a considerable hurry.

text.A2: Ask about the last tenant.
text.B1: Ask about the last tenant.
text.B2: Ask her about the last tenant.

text.A2: Look at the room itself first.
text.B1: Look at the room itself first.
text.B2: Look at the room itself first.

text.A2: "He's gone. That's all," she says. And she turns away to fix the window catch. Her voice is flat and closed. She does not want the question. Whatever happened here, she has folded it up and put it away. She will not take it out for a stranger.
text.B1: "He's gone. That's all," she says, and turns away to fuss with the window catch. Her voice is flat and closed. She doesn't want the question. Whatever happened here, she's folded it up and put it away, and won't be taking it out again for a stranger.
text.B2: "He's gone. That's all," she says, and turns away at once to busy herself with the window catch. Her voice is flat and firmly closed. She doesn't want the question, and won't have it. Whatever happened in this room, she has folded it up small and put it away somewhere, and she has no intention of taking it out again for the benefit of a stranger.

text.A2: Let it go. Ask about terms.
text.B1: Let it go; ask about the terms.
text.B2: Let it go, and ask about the terms.

text.A2: Look at what he left.
text.B1: Look more closely at what he left.
text.B2: Look more closely at what he left behind.

text.A2: The room has good light off the water. A coat is still on the hook by the door. The tin of buttons sits in the sun on the sill. Someone lived here, and not long ago. You could live here too. You can feel it. It is the first room today that has felt like a home.
text.B1: The room has good light off the water. A coat still hangs on the hook by the door; the tin of buttons catches the sun on the sill. Someone lived here, and not long ago. You could live here too — you can feel it. It's the first room today that has felt like a home at all.
text.B2: The room has good, generous light off the water. A coat still hangs on the hook by the door, and the tin of buttons catches the thin sun on the sill. Someone lived here, and not long ago, and left it warm somehow. You could live here too; you can feel it in your chest. It is the first room all day that has felt, even faintly, like a home.

text.A2: Notice the things he left.
text.B1: Notice the things he left.
text.B2: Notice the things he's left behind.

text.A2: Ask what happened here.
text.B1: Ask Halloran what happened here.
text.B2: Ask Halloran what happened here.

text.A2: Picture yourself living here.
text.B1: Picture yourself living here.
text.B2: Let yourself picture living here.

text.A2: She names the terms. The rent is fair. The deposit is steep, but not unfair. Then she says the word you were waiting for and dreading: references. "People who'll say you're sound," she says. You have been in this city three days. You know no one who could say it.
text.B1: She names the terms. The rent is fair; the deposit is steep but not unreasonable. Then comes the word you were both waiting for and dreading: references. "People who'll say you're sound," she explains. You've been in this city three days. You know no one who could say any such thing.
text.B2: She names the terms plainly. The rent is fair; the deposit is steep but not unreasonable. Then comes the word you were both waiting for and quietly dreading: references. "People who'll vouch that you're sound," she explains, as if it were the simplest thing in the world. You have been in this city precisely three days. You know no one alive here who could say it.

text.A2: Face the references problem.
text.B1: Face the references problem.
text.B2: Face the references problem head-on.

text.A2: Look around once more.
text.B1: Look around once more as she talks.
text.B2: Look around once more while she talks.

text.A2: Among his things, a notebook lies open on the sill. You look at it. Page after page of names and addresses, in a careful, patient hand. Someone wrote these to remember people by. Someone meant to write to all of them. And then, it seems, he did not get the chance.
text.B1: Among his things, a notebook lies open on the sill. You glance at it: page after page of names and addresses, in a careful, patient hand. Someone wrote these to remember people by — someone who meant to write to all of them, and then, it seems, never got the chance.
text.B2: Among his things, a notebook lies open on the sill. You glance down at it: page after page of names and addresses, all in a careful, patient hand. Someone wrote these to remember people by — someone who plainly meant to write to every one of them, and then, by the look of the half-packed room, never quite got the chance.

text.A2: Pick it up to return to him.
text.B1: Pick it up to give back to him.
text.B2: Pick it up, meaning to give it back to him.

text.A2: Leave it; not your business.
text.B1: Leave it; it's not your business.
text.B2: Leave it be; it's not your business.

text.A2: Ask Halloran about it.
text.B1: Ask Halloran about it.
text.B2: Ask Halloran about it directly.

text.A2: References. You turn the word over. You know no one in this whole city who could vouch for you. You have been here three days. Three days of stations and streets and closed doors. The one person who might speak for you is Ms Rowe. And she is your boss of three days, no more.
text.B1: References. You turn the word over in your mind. You know no one in this whole city who could vouch for you. You've been here three days — days of stations and streets and closed doors. The one person who might speak for you is Ms Rowe, and she's been your employer for all of three days.
text.B2: References. You turn the word over and over in your mind. You know no one in this entire city who could honestly vouch for you: you've been here three days, days made of cold stations and strange streets and doors closing softly in your face. The one person who might conceivably speak for you is Ms Rowe — and she has been your employer for exactly three days, no more.

text.A2: She names her condition.
text.B1: She names her one condition — unless.
text.B2: She names her one condition — unless.

text.A2: She softens a little.
text.B1: She softens a little as you take it in.
text.B2: She softens a little as she watches you take it in.

text.A2: You slip the notebook into your bag, to give back to him. It does not feel like taking. It feels like keeping it safe. Wherever he has gone, these names mattered to him once. If you ever find him, you will hand them back. Until then, you will look after them.
text.B1: You slip the notebook into your bag to give back to him. It doesn't feel like taking; it feels like keeping it safe. Wherever he's gone, these names mattered to him once. If you ever find him, you'll hand them straight back. Until then, you'll look after them for him.
text.B2: You slip the notebook into your bag, meaning to give it back to him. It doesn't feel like taking, exactly; it feels more like keeping something safe. Wherever he's gone, these names mattered to him once, enough to write down and carry. If you ever find him, you'll hand them straight back. Until then, you'll look after them for him.

text.A2: Turn back to Halloran.
text.B1: Turn back to Halloran.
text.B2: Turn back to Mrs Halloran.

text.A2: Ask her about it, holding it.
text.B1: Ask her about it, holding it.
text.B2: Ask her about it, the notebook still in your hand.

text.A2: You put the notebook down again, exactly where it lay. Whatever it is, whoever he was, it is not yours to take. You have enough to carry today without another stranger's names in your bag. You step back from the sill and turn to the room, and the woman, and the day.
text.B1: You set the notebook down again, exactly where it lay. Whatever it is, whoever he was, it's not yours to take. You have quite enough to carry today without a stranger's names in your bag. You step back from the sill and turn to the room, and the woman, and the day ahead.
text.B2: You set the notebook down again, exactly where it was lying. Whatever it is, and whoever he was, it isn't yours to take. You have more than enough to carry today without adding a stranger's carefully written names to your bag. You step back from the sill and turn instead to the room, and the woman, and the long day still ahead of you.

text.A2: Turn back to Halloran.
text.B1: Turn back to Halloran.
text.B2: Turn back to Mrs Halloran.

text.A2: Ask about him instead.
text.B1: Ask about him instead.
text.B2: Ask her about him instead.

text.A2: "No references, no room," she says. Her voice is not unkind. It is just plain. "Unless," she adds, "you give me a reason to trust my own eyes." She looks at you, waiting. This is a door held open just a crack. What you say next decides if it opens or shuts.
text.B1: "No references, no room," she says — not unkindly, just plainly. "Unless," she adds, "you give me a reason to trust my own eyes." She looks at you and waits. It's a door held open just a crack; what you say next decides whether it opens or closes.
text.B2: "No references, no room," she says, not unkindly but quite plainly. "Unless," she adds, after a moment, "you give me some reason to trust my own eyes." She looks at you steadily and waits. It's a door held open just a crack — and what you choose to say next is what decides whether it swings open or shuts in your face.

text.A2: Mention Kessler and Rowe.
text.B1: Mention Kessler and Rowe.
text.B2: Mention the firm, Kessler and Rowe.

text.A2: Just be honest about yourself.
text.B1: Just be honest about who you are.
text.B2: Just be honest about who you really are.

text.A2: She watches how you move through the room. You move carefully, as if it were already someone's home — because it is, or was. You do not touch what is not yours. Something in her grey face eases, just a little. She has seen a great many people. She knows how to read one.
text.B1: She watches how you move through the room — carefully, as if it were already someone's home, which it is, or was. You don't touch what isn't yours. Something in her grey face eases, just a little. She's seen a great many people through that door, and she knows how to read one.
text.B2: She watches, closely, how you move through the room — carefully, quietly, as if it were already someone's home, which of course it is, or lately was. You don't touch what isn't yours to touch. Something in her grey, guarded face eases, just a little. She has seen a great many people come through that door over the years, and she knows exactly how to read one.

text.A2: Mention your job at the firm.
text.B1: Mention your job at the firm.
text.B2: Mention your job at the firm.

text.A2: Be honest: new, no one, a chance.
text.B1: Be honest: new here, no one, need a chance.
text.B2: Be honest — new here, no one to vouch for you, in need of a chance.

text.A2: You mention Kessler and Rowe. Her eyebrows lift. "Rowe," she says slowly. "I know that name." She looks at you with new eyes. If Rowe would speak for you, that would change things. A name can open a door your face cannot.
text.B1: You mention Kessler and Rowe. Her eyebrows lift. "Rowe," she says slowly. "I know that name." She looks at you again with new eyes. "If she'd say a word for you, that would be a different matter." A name has opened a door your face alone couldn't.
text.B2: You mention Kessler and Rowe, and her eyebrows lift a fraction. "Rowe," she says, slowly, tasting it. "I know that name." She looks at you again, with different eyes this time. "If she'd say a word for you, well — that would be another thing entirely." A name has opened a door your face alone could never have shifted.

text.A2: A reference from the firm — how?
text.B1: A reference from the firm — but how?
text.B2: A reference from the firm — but how would you get one?

text.A2: Say you'll be honest instead.
text.B1: Say you'll just be honest instead.
text.B2: Say you'd rather just be honest with her instead.

text.A2: You tell her the plain truth. Three days in this city. No one to vouch for you. A week's pay in your pocket. You have this one day to find a home before the hotel shuts you out. You do not dress it up. You just say it, and let it stand there between you.
text.B1: You tell her the plain truth. Three days in this city, no one to vouch for you. A week's pay in your pocket, and one day to find a home before the hotel shuts you out. You don't dress it up or ask for pity. You just say it, and let it stand there between you.
text.B2: You tell her the plain truth of it. Three days in this city. No one alive here to vouch for you. A week's pay in your pocket and this one short day to find a home before the hotel shuts you out for good. You don't dress it up, and you don't ask for pity. You simply say it, and let it stand there in the good light between you.

text.A2: She says: come back at dusk.
text.B1: She says: come back at dusk.
text.B2: She tells you to come back at dusk.

text.A2: She studies you a moment more.
text.B1: She studies you a moment longer.
text.B2: She studies you a long moment more.

text.A2: "Come back when the light goes," she says. "I'll have thought by then." It is not a yes. But it is not a no. On the stair as you go down, a neighbour is struggling. She has heavy bags and a small, tired child. She is losing the fight with the stairs.
text.B1: "Come back when the light goes," she says. "I'll have thought by then." It isn't a yes; but it isn't a no, either. On the stair as you head down, a neighbour is wrestling heavy shopping bags and a small, tired child. She is plainly losing the fight with the steps.
text.B2: "Come back when the light goes," she says. "I'll have thought it over by then." It isn't a yes; but, importantly, it isn't a no either. On the stair as you head back down, a neighbour is wrestling with heavy shopping bags and a small, tired child at once, and quite plainly losing her fight with the steps.

text.A2: Fill the hours till dusk.
text.B1: Fill the hours until dusk.
text.B2: Go and fill the hours until dusk.

text.A2: Help the neighbour on the stair.
text.B1: Help the neighbour on the stair.
text.B2: Stop and help the neighbour on the stair.

text.A2: Hours to kill before dusk. A whole cold city that still does not know your name. You could go back to the square and its noise. You could sit somewhere and think ahead to the evening. Or you could add up, honestly, what this long day has already cost you.
text.B1: Hours to kill before dusk, in a whole cold city that still doesn't know your name. You could go back to the square and its noise. You could sit somewhere and think ahead to the evening. Or you could add up, honestly, what this long day has already cost you.
text.B2: Hours yet to kill before dusk, in a whole cold city that still doesn't know your name or care to. You could go back to the square and its noise. You could find somewhere quiet to sit and think ahead to the evening. Or you could sit down and add up, honestly, exactly what this long grey day has already cost you.

text.A2: Back to the square.
text.B1: Back to the square.
text.B2: Head back to the square.

text.A2: Think ahead to the evening.
text.B1: Think ahead to the evening.
text.B2: Sit and think ahead to the evening.

text.A2: Count what the day has cost.
text.B1: Count what the day has cost you.
text.B2: Add up what the day has already cost you.

text.A2: You hear the woman's story out. She paid a deposit. Vann gave her a date. Then another date. Then "so sorry, it fell through." And no money back. She has come again today, to ask for it. She will not get it. You can see that, even if she cannot yet.
text.B1: You hear the woman's story out. She paid a deposit; Vann gave her a date, then another, then "so sorry, it fell through" — and never gave the money back. She's come again today to ask for it. She won't get it. You can see that plainly, even if she can't quite let herself yet.
text.B2: You hear the woman's story out. She paid a deposit; Vann gave her a date, and then another date, and then a soft "so sorry, it fell through" — and never once gave the money back. She has come in again today to ask for it. She won't get it, and you can see that quite plainly, even if she can't yet let herself believe it.

text.A2: Thank her. Don't pay.
text.B1: Thank her and refuse to pay.
text.B2: Thank her, and refuse to pay a penny.

text.A2: Vann pushes one last time.
text.B1: Vann leans in with one last push.
text.B2: Vann leans in for one last push.

text.A2: "Last one at this price," Vann says. His hand is already out for the money. "People like you don't get second chances in this city." He means it to frighten you. And it is the tell. A real room does not need a threat to sell it. You see the trick whole now.
text.B1: "Last one at this price," Vann says, hand already out. "People like you don't get second chances in this city." He means it to frighten you into paying — and that line is the tell. A real room doesn't need a threat to sell it. You can see the whole trick now.
text.B2: "Last one at this price," Vann says, his hand already out for the money. "People like you don't get second chances in this city." He means it to frighten you into reaching for your purse — and that single line is the tell. A real room does not need a threat to sell it. You see the whole shape of the trick now, laid out plain.

text.A2: Pay, against your sense.
text.B1: Pay, against your better sense.
text.B2: Pay, against every bit of your better sense.

text.A2: That line is the tell. Leave.
text.B1: That line is the tell. Leave.
text.B2: That line is the tell — leave.

text.A2: You look back on your way out. The queue has doubled since you came in. The same warm smile, the same clock on the wall, the same open hand. New faces now, all hopeful, all tired. You are glad your money is still yours. You will not be one of them.
text.B1: You glance back on your way out. The queue has doubled since you arrived: the same warm smile, the same clock, the same open hand. But all new faces now, hopeful and tired. You're glad your money is still your own. You won't be one of them.
text.B2: You glance back on your way out. The queue has doubled since you first came in: the same warm smile, the same clock on the wall, the same open, patient hand. But all new faces now — every one of them hopeful, and tired, and a little afraid. You're glad your money is still your own. Whatever else happens today, you won't be one of them.

text.A2: On to a real room.
text.B1: On to a real room.
text.B2: On, then, to a real room.

text.A2: Think about the evening.
text.B1: Think about the evening.
text.B2: Start thinking about the evening.

text.A2: There is a better flat, across town. Clean, bright, a proper little home. But it needs a guarantor — someone to stand behind your rent if you cannot pay it. You have no such person in this city. Unless the firm would do it. Unless Ms Rowe would put her name to yours.
text.B1: There's a better flat across town — clean, bright, a proper little home. But it needs a guarantor: someone to stand behind your rent if you ever fall short. You have no such person in this city. Unless the firm would do it — unless Ms Rowe would put her name to yours.
text.B2: There's a better flat across town — clean, bright, a proper little home of the kind you'd almost stopped hoping for. But it needs a guarantor: someone willing to stand behind your rent if you ever fall short. You have no such person in this whole city. Unless the firm itself would do it — unless Ms Rowe, of all people, would put her name to yours.

text.A2: Think how to get the firm's word.
text.B1: Think how to get the firm's word.
text.B2: Work out how you might get the firm's word.

text.A2: Give up on the good flat.
text.B1: Give up on the good flat.
text.B2: Give up on the good flat entirely.

text.A2: You could ask. But it is your first week at the firm. It is a great deal to ask of people who barely know you. And yet — you did tell Ms Rowe everything, on your first night. The whole strange story. She listened to all of it, and hired you anyway.
text.B1: You could ask. But it's your first week at the firm, and it's a great deal to ask of people who barely know you. And yet — you did tell Ms Rowe everything on your first night, the whole strange story of it. She listened to every word, and hired you anyway.
text.B2: You could ask. But it's your first week at the firm, and it's a great deal to ask of people who barely know your face yet. And yet — you did tell Ms Rowe everything, on your first night here: the whole strange, exhausting story of it. She listened to every word without once interrupting, and hired you anyway. That has to count for something now.

text.A2: Call Ms Rowe, who trusts you.
text.B1: Call Ms Rowe, who trusts you.
text.B2: Call Ms Rowe, who has reason to trust you.

text.A2: Ask a colleague instead.
text.B1: Ask a colleague at the firm instead.
text.B2: Ask a colleague at the firm instead.

text.A2: Too much to ask. Let it go.
text.B1: It's too much to ask. Let it go.
text.B2: It's too much to ask in your first week. Let it go.

text.A2: You call Ms Rowe. You explain. There is a short silence. Then: "Of course. Put them onto me." That is all. No fuss, no lecture. You were straight with her once, when it would have been easier to lie. So she is straight with you now, when it matters.
text.B1: You call Ms Rowe and explain. There's a short silence, then: "Of course. Put them onto me." That's all — no fuss, no lecture. You were straight with her once, on a night when lying would have been easier. She is straight with you now, when it matters most.
text.B2: You call Ms Rowe and explain the whole thing. There's a short silence on the line, and then, simply: "Of course. Put them onto me." That's all. No fuss, no lecture, no making you ask twice. Because you were straight with her once, on a cold night when a lie would have been so much easier, she is straight with you now, without hesitation, when it matters most.

text.A2: A reference — you have one.
text.B1: A reference — you have one now.
text.B2: A reference — you have one now, and a real one.

text.A2: Thank her; get on with the day.
text.B1: Thank her and get on with the day.
text.B2: Thank her, and get on with the day.

text.A2: You ask a colleague at the firm. They hesitate — you are new, after all — but in the end they agree to say you are sound. It is not warm. It is a favour, done a little stiffly, for a near-stranger. But it is enough. A name is a name, and you have one now.
text.B1: You ask a colleague at the firm. They hesitate — you're new, after all — but in the end agree to say you're sound. It isn't warm; it's a favour done a little stiffly, for a near-stranger. But it's enough. A name is a name, and you have one now.
text.B2: You ask a colleague at the firm. They hesitate — you're new, after all, and this is a real thing to ask — but in the end they agree to say you're sound. It isn't warm, exactly; it's a favour done a little stiffly, for someone who's still very nearly a stranger. But it's enough for the letting man. A name is a name, and you have one now.

text.A2: A reference, of a kind.
text.B1: A reference, of a kind.
text.B2: A reference, of a kind, at least.

text.A2: On with the day.
text.B1: On with the day.
text.B2: On, then, with the day.

text.A2: You let the good flat go. You cannot ask the firm to put its name to yours. Not in your first week. Not when they barely know you. It is the right choice, maybe. But it is a door closing. You feel the cold of it as you turn back to the day's smaller chances.
text.B1: You let the good flat go. You can't ask the firm to put its name to yours — not in your first week, not when they barely know your face. It may be the right choice. But it's a door closing, and you feel the cold of it as you turn back to the day's smaller chances.
text.B2: You let the good flat go. You simply can't bring yourself to ask the firm to put its name to yours — not in your first week, not when they barely know your face yet. It may well be the right choice, the modest one. But it's a door closing all the same, and you feel the cold draught of it as you turn back to the day's smaller, humbler chances.

text.B2: Back to the day's smaller, real chances.

text.A2: Into the square to think.
text.B1: Into the square to think.
text.B2: Into the square to think it through.

text.A2: You have a reference now. A name that will answer for you when your own face cannot. It is a strange, warm feeling. Someone will vouch for you, in a city where you know almost no one. It changes what doors will open tonight. You carry it carefully, like the money in your pocket.
text.B1: You have a reference now — a name that will answer for you when your own face can't. It's a strange, warm feeling, being vouched for in a city where you know almost no one. It changes which doors will open tonight, and you carry it as carefully as the money in your pocket.
text.B2: You have a reference now: a name that will answer for you when your own unknown face cannot. It's a strange and genuinely warm feeling, being vouched for in a city where you know almost no one at all. It changes which doors will open to you tonight — and you carry it as carefully as you carry the money folded in your pocket.

text.A2: Carry it to the evening.

text.A2: Take the bags and help up.
text.B1: Take the bags and help her up.
text.B2: Take the bags and help her up the stairs.

text.B1: You take the heavy bags and carry them up all three floors, the child watching you gravely from below. At her door the woman is breathless with thanks. "You're a good one," she says. "I'll not forget it. Anything you need on this stair, you knock — you hear me?"
text.B2: You take the heavy, splitting bags and carry them up, all three floors, the small child watching you gravely from below. At her door the woman is breathless with gratitude. "You're a good one," she says, gripping your arm. "I'll not forget it, mind. Anything you need on this stair, ever, you knock on my door — you hear me?"

text.A2: Wave it off; back to the day.
text.B1: Wave it off and get back to the day.
text.B2: Wave it off, and get back to the day.

text.A2: She points you back to Halloran.
text.B1: She points you back toward Halloran.
text.B2: She points you back toward Halloran's door.

text.A2: You pass by with a small nod. Not unkind, just busy. You have your own day to save, and no room in it for anyone else's bags. The stair swallows the sound of her struggling up behind you. By the top, you have half-forgotten her. Almost.
text.B1: You pass by with a small nod — not unkind, just busy. You've your own day to save and no room in it for anyone else's shopping. The stair swallows the sound of her struggling up behind you, and by the top you've half-forgotten her. Almost.
text.B2: You pass her by with a small nod — not unkind, exactly, just busy. You've your own long day to save, and no room in it for a stranger's shopping. The stair swallows the sound of her struggling up behind you, and by the time you reach the top you've very nearly forgotten her. Almost, but not quite.

text.A2: Back to the day.
text.B1: Back to the day.
text.B2: On, back to the day.

text.A2: Into the square.
text.B1: Into the square.
text.B2: Into the square, then.

text.A2: You go back to the day. The good turn leaves a small warmth. Passing by leaves a small guilt. Either way, it goes with you. It is a little thing. But little things add up, in a city, into who you are in it. The light is starting, slowly, to change.
text.B1: You go back to the day, the small warmth of the good turn — or the small guilt of passing by — going with you either way. It's a little thing. But little things add up, in a city, into who you turn out to be in it. The light is beginning, slowly, to change.
text.B2: You go back to the day, and the small warmth of the good turn — or, if you passed on, the small cold guilt of it — goes with you either way. It's a little thing, easily forgotten. But little things add up, in a strange city, into who you turn out to be in it. The light is beginning, slowly and surely, to change toward evening.

text.A2: Think toward the evening.
text.B1: Think toward the evening.
text.B2: Turn your thoughts toward the evening.

text.A2: Back to Halloran's at dusk.
text.B1: Back to Halloran's block at dusk.
text.B2: Back toward Halloran's block for dusk.

text.A2: You ask Halloran, outright, what happened here. She stiffens. She straightens the coat on its hook, though it does not need it. Then she changes the subject to the rent, the stair, the water bill. The room holds its breath. There is a story here, and she is sitting on it.
text.B1: You ask Halloran outright what happened here. She stiffens. She straightens the coat on its hook, though it needs no straightening, and changes the subject to the rent, the stair, the water. The room seems to hold its breath. There's a story here, and she is sitting hard on it.
text.B2: You ask Halloran, outright, what happened in this room. She stiffens visibly. She reaches out and straightens the coat on its hook, though it doesn't need straightening at all, and then changes the subject briskly to the rent, the stair, the water bill. The room itself seems to hold its breath. There is a story here, plainly, and she is sitting on it with her whole weight.

text.A2: Press gently.
text.B1: Press her gently.
text.B2: Press her, gently.

text.A2: Let it drop.
text.B1: Let it drop.
text.B2: Let the matter drop.

text.A2: You press gently. Halloran turns away, so you turn too. On the stair, a neighbour is passing. "The lad up top?" he says, low. "Went to sea. All of a sudden. She won't speak of it." Then he is gone down the stair.
text.B1: You press gently. Halloran turns away, so you turn too — and on the stair a neighbour is passing. "The lad up top?" the neighbour murmurs. "Went to sea. All of a sudden. She won't speak of it, so don't you go asking her." And then the neighbour is gone down the stair.
text.B2: You press, gently. Halloran turns away from you, so you turn too, and on the stair a neighbour happens to be passing. "The lad up top?" the neighbour murmurs, low and quick. "Went to sea. All of a sudden, it was. She won't speak of it, so don't you go asking her." And then the neighbour, too, is gone off down the stair, and you're left holding it.

text.A2: Ask the neighbour more.
text.B1: Ask the neighbour more.
text.B2: Ask the neighbour for more.

text.A2: Leave it; help the neighbour.
text.B1: Leave it — help the neighbour instead.
text.B2: Leave it be, and help the neighbour instead.

text.A2: Back to Halloran and the room.
text.B1: Back to Halloran and the room.
text.B2: Turn back to Halloran and the room.

text.A2: "Owed nothing. Harmed no one," the neighbour says. "Just gone, one morning, with a bag. It's her boy, see. Her only one. She won't say his name now." The neighbour shakes their head, kindly. "So mind how you go, up there. That room's got more in it than furniture."
text.B1: "Owed nothing, harmed no one," the neighbour says. "Just gone one morning with a bag. It's her boy, see — her only one. She won't say his name now." They shake their head, kindly. "So mind how you go up there. That room's got more in it than furniture."
text.B2: "Owed nothing, harmed no one," the neighbour says, quietly. "Just gone, one morning, with a single bag. It's her boy, see — her only one, and grown. She won't so much as say his name now." They shake their head, not unkindly. "So mind how you go, up there. That little room's got a good deal more in it than furniture."

text.A2: Her boy. You understand now.
text.B1: Her boy. You understand the packed box now.
text.B2: Her boy — you understand the half-packed box now.

text.A2: Enough. Help with the shopping.
text.B1: Enough — help with the shopping.
text.B2: Enough of it — go and help with the shopping.

text.A2: Her son. It all makes sense now. The half-packed room she cannot finish packing. The coat she will not take down. The notebook of addresses he meant to write to, and never did. She is not hiding a crime. She is holding a door open for someone who may never come back.
text.B1: Her son. It all makes sense now. The half-packed room she can't bring herself to finish. The coat she won't take down. The notebook of addresses he meant to write to, and never did. She isn't hiding a crime. She's holding a door open for someone who may never come back.
text.B2: Her son. It all falls into place now. The half-packed room she can't bring herself to finish. The coat she won't take down from its hook. The notebook of addresses he plainly meant to write to, and never did. She isn't hiding anything shameful. She's simply holding a door open, month after month, for someone who may never walk back through it.

text.A2: Take the notebook to return it.
text.B1: Take the notebook, to return it.
text.B2: Take the notebook, meaning to return it to her.

text.A2: Say nothing; go back down.
text.B1: Say nothing, and go back down.
text.B2: Say nothing, and go quietly back down.

text.A2: At the window, you can see it. Yourself, here, in this room. The grey water below, the good light, a kettle on the ring, a life slowly built. It is the first room today that felt like more than four walls. You catch yourself hoping, and it frightens you a little.
text.B1: At the window you can see it: yourself, here, in this room. The grey water below, the good light, a kettle on the ring, a life slowly built up. It's the first room today that has felt like more than four walls. You catch yourself hoping, and the hoping frightens you a little.
text.B2: At the window you can suddenly see it all: yourself, here, in this very room. The grey water sliding below, the good clean light, a kettle on the ring, a whole life quietly built up over time. It's the first room all day that has felt like more than four walls and a price. You catch yourself hoping, properly hoping, and the hope frightens you a little.

text.A2: Look at what he left behind.
text.B1: Look at what he left behind.
text.B2: Look again at what he left behind.

text.A2: Turn back before you hope too much.
text.B1: Turn back before you hope too hard.
text.B2: Turn away before you let yourself hope too hard.

text.A2: In the coat pocket, your fingers find a photograph. It is this same window. A young man stands at it, laughing. Beside him is Halloran — younger, softer, laughing too. You should not have looked. But now you have, and you cannot un-see whose room this is.
text.B1: In the coat pocket your fingers find a photograph. It's this same window — a young man standing at it, laughing, and beside him Halloran, younger and softer, laughing too. You shouldn't have looked. But now you have, and you can't un-see whose room this really is.
text.B2: In the coat pocket your fingers close on a photograph. It's this same window — a young man standing at it, laughing at whoever held the camera, and beside him Halloran herself, years younger and softer, laughing too. You know you shouldn't have looked. But now you have, and there's no un-seeing it, and no pretending you don't know whose room this is.

text.A2: You understand who lived here.
text.B1: You understand who lived here.
text.B2: You understand, now, who lived here.

text.A2: Put it back exactly as it was.
text.B1: Put it back exactly as it was.
text.B2: Put it back exactly where it was.

text.A2: Someone lived here, and left fast. The woman letting the room is no stranger to him. She is his mother. She lets his room to keep the rent coming in. She keeps his coat on the hook. That way the room is never quite empty of him. You hold all of this now, quietly.
text.B1: Someone lived here and left fast, and the woman letting the room is no stranger to him at all — she is his mother. She lets his room to keep the rent coming in. She keeps his coat on the hook, so the place is never quite empty of him. You hold all of that now, quietly.
text.B2: Someone lived here, and left in a hurry, and the grey-eyed woman letting the room is no stranger to him at all: she is his mother. She lets his room out to keep the rent coming in, and keeps his coat on its hook so that the place is never, quite, empty of him. You hold all of that now, quietly, and it changes how you'll speak to her.

text.A2: Take the notebook to give back.
text.B1: Take the notebook, to give it back.
text.B2: Take the notebook, meaning to give it back to her.

text.A2: Say nothing yet.
text.B1: Say nothing of it yet.
text.B2: Say nothing of it yet.

text.A2: Dania wants to see a place round the corner first. You go with her. It is small, and dark, and not right for her. But she has to see it to know that. This is how looking works. You walk it with her. Two lost people are still two, and that helps.
text.B1: Dania wants to see a place round the corner first, so you go with her. It's small and dark and not right for her — but she has to see it to know that; this is how looking works. You walk it with her anyway. Two lost people are still two, and that helps a little.
text.B2: Dania wants to see a place round the corner first, so you go along with her. It's small, and dark, and plainly not right for her — but she has to see it with her own eyes to know that, because this is simply how the looking works. You walk it with her anyway, uncomplaining. Two lost people are still, at least, two, and on a day like this that helps more than a little.

text.A2: On to the canal room after.
text.B1: On to the canal room after.
text.B2: On to the canal room after this.

text.A2: She's found something; you haven't.
text.B1: She's found something; you're still looking.
text.B2: She's found something of her own; you're still looking.

text.A2: Dania takes a small room she likes, and hugs you goodbye. You are glad for her, honestly glad. But when she is gone, the day feels wider and colder. You are more alone in it than before. One of you has a home tonight. The other is still walking.
text.B1: Dania takes a small room she likes and hugs you goodbye. You're glad for her — honestly glad. But once she's gone the day feels wider and colder, and you're more alone in it than before. One of you has a home tonight. The other is still walking the streets.
text.B2: Dania takes a small room she likes the look of, and hugs you goodbye on the pavement. You're glad for her — honestly, uncomplicatedly glad. But once she's gone the day feels suddenly wider and colder, and you're more alone in it than you were before you met her this morning. One of you has a home tonight. The other is still out walking the streets.

text.A2: Back to the square.
text.B1: Back to the square.
text.B2: Head back to the square.

text.A2: On to the evening.
text.B1: On to the evening.
text.B2: On, then, to the evening.

text.A2: She texts you a listing.
text.B1: She texts you a listing to try.
text.B2: She texts you a listing to try before it goes.

text.A2: You offer to mind the child while she wrestles the bags. The child takes your hand and holds it, solemn and trusting, the way small children do. It is a tiny trust, freely given, and it warms you more than you expect. Together, the three of you make slow progress up.
text.B1: You offer to mind the child while she wrestles the bags. The child takes your hand and holds it, solemn and trusting, the way small children do without thinking. It's a tiny trust, freely given, and it warms you more than you'd expect. Together, the three of you make slow progress up.
text.B2: You offer to mind the child while she wrestles the splitting bags. The child takes your hand at once and holds it, solemn and entirely trusting, the way small children give their trust without thinking to weigh it. It's a tiny thing, freely given, and it warms you rather more than you'd expect it to. Together, the three of you make slow, careful progress up the stairs.

text.A2: See them both safely up.
text.B1: See them both safely up.
text.B2: See them both safely up to the top.

text.A2: Hand the child back; hurry on.
text.B1: Hand the child back and hurry on.
text.B2: Hand the child back, and hurry on.

text.A2: Dusk. The hotel wants its room back tonight. You have one evening left, and whatever the day has given you. Money, maybe. A name to vouch for you, maybe. Or only tired feet and a cold nose. Where do you go first, while there is still light to go by?
text.B1: Dusk. The hotel wants its room back tonight, and there's no more time. You have one evening left, and whatever the long day has given you — money kept, a name to vouch for you, or only tired feet. Where do you go first, while there's still light to go by?
text.B2: Dusk. The hotel wants its room back tonight, and there is no more time to play with. You have one evening left, and whatever the long day has handed you: money kept, perhaps, or a name to vouch for you, or only tired feet and a cold nose. Where do you go first, while there is still a little light to go by?

text.A2: Back to Mrs Halloran's.
text.B1: Back to Mrs Halloran's.
text.B2: Back to Mrs Halloran's.

text.A2: Claim the good flat.
text.B1: Claim the good flat.
text.B2: Go and claim the good flat.

text.A2: Weigh the other options.
text.B1: Weigh the other options.
text.B2: Weigh up the other options.

text.A2: The light is nearly gone. You think about what is really in your reach tonight. Not dreams. Not the good flat you cannot afford. What can your hands actually close on, before the dark? You look at what you have, and what you did today, and you weigh it.
text.B1: The light is nearly gone. You think hard about what's actually within your reach tonight. Not dreams, not the good flat you can't afford, but what your hands can really close on before dark. You look at what you have, and what you did today, and you weigh it.
text.B2: The light is nearly gone. You think hard about what's actually within your reach tonight. Not dreams, and not the good flat you can't afford — only what your hands can really close on before the dark comes down. You look at what you have, and at what you did today, and you weigh the two together.

text.A2: Go for the agent's keys.
text.B1: Go for the agent's keys.
text.B2: Go for the agent's keys.

text.A2: Sign for the bedsit.
text.B1: Sign for the bedsit.
text.B2: Go and sign for the bedsit.

text.A2: One last phone check.
text.B1: One last phone check.
text.B2: One last check of the phone.

text.A2: None of these. Think again.
text.B1: None of these — think again.
text.B2: None of these — think again.

text.A2: Nothing has quite worked today. The hotel closes its door to you at ten o'clock. You are nearly out of choices, and nearly out of light. But not quite. There may be one more door to knock on. Or there may only be the long, cold thought of leaving this city.
text.B1: Nothing has quite worked today, and the hotel shuts its door to you at ten. You're nearly out of choices and nearly out of light — but not quite. There may still be one more door worth knocking on. Or there may only be the long, cold thought of leaving.
text.B2: Nothing has quite worked today, and the hotel shuts its door to you at ten o'clock sharp. You're nearly out of choices, and nearly out of light — but not, yet, entirely. There may still be one last door worth the knocking. Or there may only be the long, cold thought of leaving this city the way you came.

text.A2: Ask the neighbour you helped.
text.B1: Ask the neighbour you helped.
text.B2: Ask the neighbour you helped this morning.

text.A2: Try the landlady who knew your name.
text.B1: Try the landlady who remembered your name.
text.B2: Try the landlady who remembered your name.

text.A2: Accept the rooms are gone.
text.B1: Accept the rooms are gone for today.
text.B2: Accept the rooms are gone for the day.

text.A2: Wonder if the city will have you.
text.B1: Wonder if this city will ever have you.
text.B2: Wonder whether this city will ever have you.

text.A2: You sit on a cold bench and add the day up. The bus fares you spent. The wasted trip out of town. The rooms you saw. And the one room by the water that felt, for a moment, like a home. The light is going now. You have to choose where to spend the last of it.
text.B1: You sit on a cold bench and add the day up. The fares spent, the wasted trip out of town, the grim rooms seen. And the one room by the water that felt, for a moment, like a home. The light is going now. You have to choose where to spend the last of it.
text.B2: You sit on a cold bench and add the day up honestly. The fares spent, the wasted trip out of town, the grim rooms seen. And the one room by the water that felt, just for a moment, like a home. The light is going now, and going fast. You have to choose where to spend the very last of it.

text.A2: Decide where to go as the light goes.
text.B1: Decide where to go as the light goes.
text.B2: Decide where to go while the light lasts.

text.A2: None of it's enough. Think harder.
text.B1: None of it's enough — think harder.
text.B2: None of it's quite enough — think harder.

text.A2: The stalls are closing around you.
text.B1: The stalls are closing around you.
text.B2: The stalls are folding up around you.

text.A2: You climb Halloran's stair again. The light in her window has just come on. It is warm and yellow against the grey evening. Your feet are heavy, and your heart is louder than it should be. This is the room you want. You knew it at noon. You know it now.
text.B1: You climb Halloran's stair again. The light in her window has just come on, warm and yellow against the grey evening. Your feet are heavy, and your heart is louder than it should be. This is the room you want — you knew it at noon, and you know it now.
text.B2: You climb Halloran's stair again in the failing light. The lamp in her window has just come on, warm and yellow against the grey of the evening. Your feet are heavy, and your heart is beating louder than it has any need to. This is the room you want. You knew it at noon, and you know it still.

text.A2: She opens the door.
text.B1: She opens the door.
text.B2: She opens the door.

text.A2: Give back his notebook first.
text.B1: Give back his notebook first.
text.B2: Give back his notebook first.

text.A2: The walk up feels longer at dusk.
text.B1: The walk up feels longer at dusk.
text.B2: The climb feels longer at dusk.

text.A2: The good flat is clean and bright and real. A little home, up two flights, with a window that gets the morning. The letting man barely looks at you. He only wants your reference to be real, and it is. There is nothing here to fear, and nothing hidden. Just a door, and a key.
text.B1: The good flat is clean and bright and real — a proper little home, two flights up, with a window that catches the morning. The letting man barely looks at you; he only needs your reference to be real, and it is. There's nothing hidden here, nothing to fear. Just a door and a key.
text.B2: The good flat is clean and bright and unmistakably real — a proper little home, two flights up, with a window that catches the morning light. The letting man barely looks at you; he only needs your reference to be genuine, and it is. There is nothing hidden here, and nothing to fear. Just a door, and a key, and your own name on the paper.

text.A2: Take it; you're vouched for.
text.B1: Take it; you're vouched for.
text.B2: Take it — you're vouched for.

text.A2: Hesitate; it's a lot to hold.
text.B1: Hesitate — it's more than you can hold.
text.B2: Hesitate — it feels like more than you can hold.

text.A2: You have Vann's address at last. It is a slip of cheap paper and a cold key. The street name means nothing to you. The key is heavy and strange in your hand. Somewhere out there, he promised, is your room. You have paid for it already. Now you go to find it.
text.B1: You have Vann's address at last — a slip of cheap paper and a cold, heavy key. The street name means nothing to you. Somewhere out there, he promised, is the room you already paid for. You button your coat against the dark and go to find it.
text.B2: You have Vann's address at last: a slip of cheap paper and a cold, heavy key that means nothing yet. The street name is one you've never heard. Somewhere out there, he promised, warmly, is the room you have already paid most of a week's wage for. You button your coat against the dark, and go to find it.

text.A2: Go and let yourself in.
text.B1: Go and let yourself in.
text.B2: Go and let yourself in.

text.A2: Hesitate on the dark street.
text.B1: Hesitate on the dark street.
text.B2: Hesitate a moment on the dark street.

text.A2: The bedsit landlord counts your cash again, slowly, and pushes a scrap of paper across for your name. No lease. No handshake. No welcome. Just a room with a wall for a view, and a shared bathroom down a cold stair. It is a room. Tonight, a room is what you need.
text.B1: The bedsit landlord counts your cash again, slowly, then pushes a scrap of paper across for your name. No lease, no handshake, no welcome — just a room with a wall for a view and a shared bathroom down a cold stair. It's a room. Tonight, a room is what you need.
text.B2: The bedsit landlord counts your cash again, slowly, and then pushes a scrap of paper across the table for your name. No lease, no handshake, no welcome of any kind — just a room with a blank wall for a view and a shared bathroom down a cold stair. It is a room, all the same. And tonight, a room is what you need.

text.A2: Sign; it's yours tonight.
text.B1: Sign; it's yours tonight.
text.B2: Sign — it's yours tonight.

text.A2: Back out at the last second.
text.B1: Back out at the last second.
text.B2: Back out at the very last second.

text.A2: Mrs Halloran stands in the doorway. Behind her, the room is warm and lit. The deposit money is warm too, folded tight in your hand. She looks at you and waits. She is not a woman who fills a silence for you. Whatever happens next, you will have to begin it.
text.B1: Mrs Halloran stands in the doorway, the warm room lit behind her, the deposit money folded tight and warm in your hand. She looks at you and waits. She isn't a woman who'll fill a silence for you. Whatever happens next, you'll have to be the one to begin it.
text.B2: Mrs Halloran stands in the doorway, the warm room lit behind her, the deposit money folded tight and warm in your hand. She looks at you and waits. She isn't the kind of woman who will fill a silence on your behalf. Whatever happens next, you are the one who is going to have to begin it.

text.A2: Talk terms.
text.B1: Talk terms.
text.B2: Talk terms.

text.A2: Step back onto the stair a moment.
text.B1: Step back onto the stair a moment.
text.B2: Step back onto the stair for a moment.

text.A2: She waits. This is the moment the whole long day has been walking toward. You can tell her the plain truth about yourself — new, alone, with no one behind you. Or you can keep it safe and small. Just the rent, just the dates, nothing that costs you anything to say.
text.B1: She waits. This is the moment the whole long day has been walking toward. You can tell her the plain truth about yourself — new, alone, with no one at your back. Or you can keep it safe and businesslike: just the rent, just the dates, nothing that costs you anything to say.
text.B2: She waits. This is the moment the whole long day has been walking toward. You can tell her the plain truth of yourself — new, alone, with no one at all standing behind you. Or you can keep it safe and businesslike: just the rent, just the dates, nothing that costs you a thing to say aloud.

text.A2: Tell her the truth about yourself.
text.B1: Tell her the truth of your circumstances.
text.B2: Tell her the plain truth of your circumstances.

text.A2: Keep it businesslike; just the rent.
text.B1: Keep it businesslike; just the rent.
text.B2: Keep it businesslike — just the rent.

text.A2: You tell her the truth, all of it. New to the city. Alone. A week's pay and no one to vouch for you. But honest, and careful, and someone who will look after her room like it matters. Her grey eyes hold yours the whole time. She does not look away.
text.B1: You tell her the truth of it, plainly. New to the city, alone, a week's pay and no one to vouch for you. But honest, and careful, and someone who'll look after her room as if it mattered. Her grey eyes hold yours the whole time. She doesn't look away once.
text.B2: You tell her the truth of it, plainly and without decoration. New to the city, alone, a week's pay and no one alive here to vouch for you. But honest, and careful, and someone who will look after her room as though it mattered. Her grey eyes hold yours the whole time. She does not look away once.

text.A2: She decides.
text.B1: She decides.
text.B2: She decides.

text.A2: Retreat to business after all.
text.B1: On second thought, retreat to business.
text.B2: On second thought, retreat to business.

text.A2: You keep it to rent and dates and deposits. It is correct. It is cool. You give her nothing of yourself, because giving things away has hurt before. She nods along and writes nothing down. Something in the room stays shut, and you feel it stay shut, and you say nothing.
text.B1: You keep it to rent and dates and deposits — correct, cool, careful. You give her nothing of yourself, because giving yourself away has cost you before. She nods along and writes nothing down. Something in the room stays shut, and you feel it stay shut, and you let it.
text.B2: You keep it strictly to rent and dates and deposits — correct, cool, careful. You give her nothing of yourself, because giving yourself away has cost you before, more than once. She nods along and writes nothing down. Something in the room stays shut the whole time, and you feel it stay shut, and you let it.

text.A2: She weighs it.
text.B1: She weighs it.
text.B2: She weighs it up.

text.A2: Change tack; be honest after all.
text.B1: Change tack; be honest after all.
text.B2: Change tack — be honest after all.

text.A2: You find the street. It is a car park behind a builder's hoarding. There is no building. There is no door. There is no room, and there never was one. The key in your hand fits nothing at all. You stand in the cold and understand, slowly, exactly what you have done.
text.B1: You find the street. It's a car park behind a builder's hoarding — no building, no door, no room, and there never was one. The key in your hand fits nothing at all. You stand there in the cold and understand, slowly, exactly what you've done.
text.B2: You find the street at last. It's a car park behind a builder's hoarding — no building, no door, no room, and, you understand now, there never was one. text.A2: The deposit is gone.

text.A2: You look at your phone one last time. The good rooms are all marked LET now. They are gone. Only the bright, cheap, lying ones are still there — Vann's kind, smiling out of the screen. The real ones went while you were walking. There is nothing here for you now.
text.B1: You scroll your phone one last time. The good rooms are all marked LET now — gone while you were out walking. Only the bright, cheap, lying ones are still up, Vann's kind, smiling out of the screen. There's nothing real left here tonight.

text.A2: The market folds up around you. Traders pull down shutters. They stack crates and sweep the ground. The day is packing itself away, and it did not find you a home. You could follow the evening wherever it leads. Or you could sit here, and let the city win, just for a moment.

text.B2: The market folds up around you — shutters coming down, crates stacked, the ground swept, the whole smell of a day ending. It has packed itself neatly away without troubling to find you a home. You could follow the evening wherever it happens to lead. Or you could sit down right here, and let the city win, just for a moment.

text.A2: Go where the evening leads.
text.B1: Go where the evening leads.
text.B2: Go where the evening leads.

text.A2: A light comes down the stair to meet you. She heard your feet on the steps. Mrs Halloran does not call out. She just waits, with the lamp, in the doorway above. There is nothing to do now but go up. Go up, meet her, and say what you came to say.
text.B1: A light comes down the stair to meet you — she heard your feet on the steps. Mrs Halloran doesn't call out; she just waits with the lamp in the doorway above. There's nothing to do now but go up, meet her, and say what you came to say.

text.B1: You read Vann's receipt again, slowly. The company name means nothing — you can't find it listed anywhere — and the phone number just rings and rings. The cold doubt hardens into something worse, something like knowledge. You gave that man most of a week's pay for a slip of paper.
text.B2: You read Vann's receipt over again, slowly this time. The company name means nothing — you can't find it listed anywhere at all — and the phone number simply rings and rings into silence. The cold doubt in your chest hardens into something worse, something uncomfortably like knowledge. You gave that man most of a week's pay in exchange for a printed slip of paper.

text.A2: Try to salvage the day.

text.A2: Dania's text comes through: a room near hers, going tonight. It is kind of her to think of you. But "going tonight" is a hard promise to catch. Her part of the city is a long, cold way from here. It is probably gone already. Probably. But maybe not.
text.B1: Dania's text comes through: a room near hers, going tonight. Kind of her to think of you. But 'going tonight' is a hard promise to catch, and her part of the city is a long cold way off. It's probably gone already. Probably. But maybe not.

But 'going tonight' is a very hard promise to catch, and her part of the city is a long, cold way from where you're standing. It's probably gone already. Probably. But then again — maybe, just maybe, not.

text.A2: The last of the light lies on the wet square. Somewhere close, a door is warm, and a room is lit, and someone is home. The question is only whether one of them is warm for you. You have one idea left, or none. You stand, and you decide which.

text.B2: The last of the light lies on the wet square. Somewhere close a door is warm, a room is lit, someone is safely home. The only real question left is whether one of them, tonight, is warm for you. You have one idea left, or perhaps none at all. You stand up, and decide which it is.

text.A2: She stands back and opens the door wide. "Then you'd better come in out of the cold," she says. That is all. That is everything. The room is yours — the good light, the water below, the window you will learn by heart. Your first job at the firm was fixing the letters. Your first job here is the window catch. You are home.
text.B1: She steps back and opens the door wide. "Then you'd better come in out of the cold," she says — and that is all, and that is everything. The room is yours: the good light, the grey water below, the window you'll come to know by heart. Your first job at the firm was fixing the letters. Your first job here is the window catch. You are home.
text.B2: She steps back and opens the door wide. "Then you'd better come in out of the cold," she says — and that is all of it, and that is everything. The room is yours: the good clean light, the grey water sliding below, the window you'll come to know by heart. Your first job at the firm was fixing the letters. Your first job here is the window catch. You are home, and the word means something again.

text.A2: She takes the notebook and sits down hard on the packed box. For a long time she says nothing. Then she tells you: her son, gone to sea, no word in a year. These were his people, the ones he meant to write. "You brought a piece of him back," she says at last. The room is yours. So, now, is a place at her table.
text.B1: She takes the notebook and sits down hard on the half-packed box. For a long while she says nothing at all. Then it comes out: her son, gone to sea, not a word from him in a year. These were the people he meant to write to. "You've brought a piece of him back," she says at last. The room is yours — and so, now, is a place at her table.
text.B2: She takes the notebook and sits down hard on the half-packed box, as if her legs had simply stopped. For a long while she says nothing at all. Then it comes out, quietly: her son, gone to sea, not a single word from him in a year. These were the people he meant to write to, and never did. "You've brought a piece of him back to me," she says at last. The room is yours — and so, now, is a place at her table.

text.A2: No favours. No con. No one to vouch for you. Just a small, real room. You took it with money you kept safe all day, coin by coin. The walls are bare and the chair is borrowed. But the key is yours, and only yours. You earned every part of it. Tonight you sleep in a room that owes nobody anything.
text.B1: No favours, no con, no one vouching for you. Just a small, real room, taken with money you kept safe all day — coin by coin, mile by walked mile. The walls are bare and the chair is borrowed. But the key is yours, and only yours, and you earned every part of it. Tonight you sleep in a room that owes nobody anything.
text.B2: No favours, no con, and no one at all vouching for you. Just a small, real room, taken with money you kept safe the whole day — coin by careful coin, mile by walked mile. The walls are bare and the one chair is borrowed. But the key is yours, and only yours, and you earned every last part of it. Tonight you sleep in a room that owes nobody anything.

text.A2: Ms Rowe's word unlocks the door. One sentence from her, and the good flat is yours — the flat you could never have taken alone. You are still new here. You still know almost no one. But you are known now, by one person who matters. That turns out to be the thing that opens doors. You go up to your own window.
text.B1: Ms Rowe's word unlocks the door. One sentence from her and the good flat is yours — the flat you could never have taken on your own. You're still new here, and you still know almost no one. But you're known now, by one person who counts, and that, it turns out, is what opens doors. You climb up to your own window.
text.B2: Ms Rowe's word unlocks the door. One sentence from her, and the good flat is yours — the flat you could never have taken on your own. You're still new to the city, and you still know almost no one in it. But you are known now, by one person who counts, and being known, you're learning, is exactly how a stranger turns slowly into a resident. You climb up to your own window.

text.A2: You took the first thing, sight barely seen. It is yours now. It is fine. It is grey, and quiet, and empty. You lie on the bed with your coat still on and listen to strangers on the stair. You have a room. You wanted a home. Tonight you learn, in the cold, that the two are not the same thing.
text.B1: You took the first thing going, sight barely seen. It's yours now, and it's fine, and it's grey and quiet and empty. You lie on the bed with your coat still on, listening to strangers move about on the stair. You have a room. You wanted a home. Tonight you learn, lying there, that the two are not the same thing at all.
text.B2: You took the first thing going, sight barely seen, because you were tired and afraid of the dark. It's yours now, and it's fine, and it's grey and quiet and utterly empty. You lie on the bed with your coat still on, listening to strangers move about on the stair. You have a room. You wanted a home. Tonight you learn, lying there in the cold, exactly how far apart the two things are.

text.A2: No room of your own tonight. But there is a box room at the back of a stranger's flat, warm and small. And a child who says a shy hello. You carried her bags this morning and forgot it by noon. She did not forget. It is not a home yet. But it is warmth, and a door that opens to you. Tonight, that is far from nothing.
text.B1: No room of your own tonight. But there's a box room at the back of a stranger's flat — warm, small, and offered freely. You carried her shopping this morning and forgot it by noon; she didn't forget it at all. It isn't a home, not yet. But it's warmth, and a door that opens to you, and tonight that is a very long way from nothing.
text.B2: No room of your own tonight. But there's a box room at the back of a stranger's flat — warm, small, and offered without a second thought. You carried her shopping up three flights this morning and had forgotten it by noon; she, it turns out, did not forget it at all. It isn't a home, not yet. But it's warmth, and a door that opens to you, and on a night like this that is a very long way from nothing.

text.A2: No room today. But at the last door, the landlady looks at you and says your name. She remembers you from the morning. "Come back Monday," she says. "I may have something then." It is not a bed for tonight. But it is a small, real thing: you are becoming someone this city knows. That is a kind of address.
text.B1: No room today. But at the last door, the landlady looks at you and says your name — she remembers you from the morning. "Come back Monday," she says. "I may have something by then." It's no bed for tonight. But it's a small, real thing: you're becoming someone this city knows. And that is a kind of address.
text.B2: No room today. But at the last door of the day, the landlady looks at you and says your name — she remembers you from the morning, out of all the faces. "Come back Monday," she says. "I may well have something by then." It's no bed for tonight. But it's a small, real thing all the same: you are slowly becoming someone this city knows by name. And that, in the end, is its own kind of address.

text.A2: Nothing signed today. But you did not lose your money, and you did not lose your head. You know the city's map now, and its prices, and its tricks. You buy one more week at the hotel and set your alarm for early. It is not a loss. It is a day spent learning the ground. Tomorrow you look again, and better.
text.B1: Nothing signed today — but you didn't lose your money, and you didn't lose your head. You know the city's map now, its prices, its tricks. You buy one more week at the hotel and set the alarm for early. It isn't a loss; it's a day spent learning the ground. Tomorrow you look again, and look better.
text.B2: Nothing signed today — but you didn't lose your money, and, just as importantly, you didn't lose your head. You know the city's map now, and its prices, and its handful of tricks. You buy yourself one more week at the hotel and set the alarm for early. It isn't a loss; it's a day spent learning the ground under your feet. Tomorrow you'll look again, and look better.

text.A2: The room was never his to let. You know that now, standing in the dark with a key that fits no door. The money — most of a week's pay — is gone, and it is not coming back. The hotel wants its key by ten. You knew the tune. You heard it once before, on your first night. And still you danced to it.
text.B1: The room was never his to let — you understand that now, standing in the dark with a key that opens nothing. The money, most of a week's pay, is gone, and it isn't coming back. The hotel wants its key by ten. You knew this tune; you heard it once before, on your first night. And you danced to it anyway.
text.B2: The room was never his to let, and you understand that completely now, standing in the dark with a key that opens nothing at all. The money — most of a week's hard pay — is gone, and it is not coming back. The hotel wants its key by ten. You knew this tune; you heard it played once already, on your first night in the city. And you danced to it anyway.

text.A2: No money kept. No name to vouch for you. Nothing at all to set against a stranger's tired face. Every good door today was a polite no, said kindly, and shut all the same. You did nothing wrong. You were just new, and alone, and the day was too short for that. The light is gone, and so is your chance.
text.B1: No money kept, no name to vouch for you, nothing at all to set against a stranger's tired face. Every good door today was a polite no — said kindly enough, and shut all the same. You did nothing wrong. You were simply new, and alone, and the day was too short for that. The light is gone now, and so is your chance.
text.B2: No money kept, no name to vouch for you, and nothing at all to set against a stranger's tired face. Every good door in the city today was a polite no — said kindly enough, and shut all the same. You did nothing wrong. You were simply new, and alone, and the short winter day was never going to be long enough for that. The light is gone now, and your chance has gone with it.

text.A2: You spent the daylight on the wrong lead, and now it is gone. By the time you turned back, the real rooms were already taken. The city did not cheat you today. You simply ran out of light, and light was the one thing you could not buy back. You walk to the dark hotel to beg one more night.
text.B1: You spent the daylight chasing the wrong lead, and now the daylight is gone. By the time you turned back, the real rooms had all been taken. The city didn't cheat you today — you simply ran out of light, and light was the one thing you couldn't buy back. You trudge to the hotel to beg one more night.
text.B2: You spent the whole of the daylight chasing the wrong lead, and now the daylight is simply gone. By the time you turned back toward the real rooms, every one of them had been taken. The city didn't cheat you today — you merely ran out of light, and light was the one thing you couldn't buy back at any price. You trudge to the darkened hotel to beg one more night.

text.A2: No room. No welcome. And then the old thought comes again, the one from your first night. A two-o'clock train. A way back to a place where they know your face. You stand on that cold platform in your mind and feel how easy it would be. You do not buy the ticket. Not yet. But tonight, for the first time, you truly think about it.
